paras: The lynching of Alexander Thompson took place at Gurdon, Arkansas, early on April 23, 1903, when a disguised mob took Thompson, a Black lumber-mill worker, from the town calaboose and hanged him from a railroad trestle. He had been held on a charge of cutting a physician, Dr. J. H. Guffman, in a dispute over a medical bill. A coroner's jury blamed unknown parties, and the local lumber plant shut down when its Black laborers quit work. Wire reports stressed that the lynching was done quietly, which some headline writers turned to irony.

Thompson worked in the dry house of the Gurdon Lumber Company's mill, in a town whose Black population of about 750 was, according to a follow-up dispatch, as large as its white population. On April 22 he quarrelled with Dr. Guffman (Cuffman in some versions) over a bill for medical services and cut the doctor about the neck; accounts of how the fight began differ.

Thompson was placed in the calaboose, where, according to the Arkansas Gazette's correspondent, extra guards were posted. At about 12:30 a.m. what the Gazette called "a party of supposed white men" overpowered the guards and took him away; the Gazette added that Black men were later seen hunting for the party. About six o'clock that morning Haywood Dickinson, a Black worker on his way to the mill, found the body hanging from the Caney Creek trestle on the Iron Mountain line, half a mile north of town.

A coroner's jury empaneled that morning questioned the guards who had been on duty. They testified that the mob's members wore their coats inside out and handkerchiefs over their eyes, said nothing, and could not be identified as white or Black. The jury returned a verdict of death "at the hands of unknown parties," and no report of arrests appears in the coverage.

The lumber plant closed that day for want of hands, the sheriff stayed in town, and guards were posted overnight. Thompson's brother arrived and, the local dispatch said, was "looked upon with suspicion," while the doctor was reported to be recovering.

The Washington Evening Star carried the wire story on April 23, and by the next day it ran in papers from Maine to Utah. The wire text said "the lynching was performed quietly and no excitement prevails," and the Portland Daily Press headed it "A Quiet Home Lynching. Little Affair in Arkansas Without Undue Noise," while the Indianapolis Journal put "affair" in quotation marks. Other headlines departed from the text: the Salt Lake Herald called Thompson a "murderer" though the doctor survived, and the Wheeling Register said he was hanged "to a pole."

Papers using the Gazette's dispatch led with racial conflict, as in "Negro Mob Pursuing White Mob in Arkansas" in the Americus Times-Recorder. In Arkansas the Newport Weekly Independent's account called Thompson "a very bad negro," and the Sharp County Record remarked that the state had given "the Cape Cod and Kalamazoo papers" cause for an extra. The Birmingham Age-Herald, by contrast, wrote that a man "who disputed a doctor's bill was lynched in Arkansas. Thus anarchy marches steadily on."

In the Black press, the Baltimore Afro-American reported on May 2 that Thompson was lynched "for striking a white man" and that "the white man lives while Thompson is in his grave," shifting attention from the bill to the gap between offense and punishment. In August the Seattle Republican listed him under April 23 in "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign," and the Sedalia Times gave his offense as "assault."

The Arkansas Democrat's correspondent, whose text the wire carried, said Thompson refused to pay and slashed the doctor "from ear to ear, just missing the jugular vein." The Gazette's correspondent wrote instead that Thompson called the doctor a liar, that Guffman struck him with a paperweight, and that Thompson then cut him three times in the back of the neck. The Gazette's "supposed white men" also conflicts with the guards' inquest testimony that the mob's race could not be told.
Most reports placed the hanging at the trestle, but the German-language Arkansas Echo said a telegraph pole, and the Malvern Times-Journal dated the lynching to the 22nd rather than the 23rd.

Thompson was taken from custody and hanged by a 'mob' whose 'members' overpowered the guards (A3, A23), with no lawful authority; the papers tie it to the charge that he cut Dr. Guffman (A1, A2, A24).

Separate Arkansas Democrat and Arkansas Gazette specials (A2, A3), a local Gurdon dispatch with inquest testimony (A23), and the Baltimore Afro-American (A28) agree that Thompson was taken from jail and lynched.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire text stressing that 'the lynching was performed quietly and no excitement prevails'.
Northern headline writers mocked the 'quiet' framing: 'A Quiet Home Lynching. Little Affair in Arkansas Without Undue Noise' (Portland) and 'Quiet Arkansas "Affair."' (Indianapolis).
The Salt Lake Herald headed the story 'Murderer Strung Up by Mob in Arkansas' although the doctor survived.
Gazette-based versions led with racial conflict: 'Another Race Difficulty', 'Negro Mob Pursuing White Mob in Arkansas'.
The Newport Weekly Independent's local account called Thompson 'a very bad negro' and blamed 'bullies among the negroes'.
Birmingham Age-Herald editorial paragraph: 'Thus anarchy marches steadily on.'
Baltimore Afro-American: 'The white man lives while Thompson is in his grave.'
Seattle Republican listed him in 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign'; Sedalia Times in a 'Record of Lynching'.

record_check.dossier: The altercation was April 22; the mob took Thompson about 12:30 a.m. April 23 and the body was found that morning, so the lynching itself falls on April 23 (night of April 22-23).
No article names the county; only 'the Sheriff of the County' is mentioned.
The local Gurdon dispatch and Arkansas weeklies spell it Gurdon; the wire used Guerdon, the Democrat special Gordon.

Gurdon (also printed Guerdon, Gordon, Gourdon), Arkansas; hanged from the Caney Creek trestle on the Iron Mountain main line, about half a mile north of town (one German-language report says a telegraph pole).
Alexander (Alex) Thompson, described as 'a negro'/'colored', employed in the dry house at the Gurdon Lumber Company mill.

Accused of cutting Dr. J. H. Guffman (Cuffman) in the neck in a dispute over a bill for medical services; the Gazette version says the doctor struck him first with a paperweight; the Afro-American says 'striking a white man'; the Sedalia Times list says 'assault'.
Unidentified mob; the Gazette called them 'supposed white men'; guards testified the race of the members could not be told.
